messages.subject: Hayes Model 21 in lavaan: how to implement second stage interaction
messages.subject_clean: Hayes Model 21 in lavaan: how to implement second stage interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hi there

I am currently looking for a way to implement hayes Model 21 (see picture, from http://www.personal.psu.edu/jxb14/M554/specreg/templates.pdf), a moderated mediation with 2 moderators.
How can I implement the second stage interaction of the mediator with the moderator? Is there a way to create the Interaction within the model? Right now I am creating the interaction beforehand in the dataframe, which is ok for the first-stage interaction, as it comes directly from the data - but for the second stage (correct me if I am wrong), I would need to draw on the regressed mediator?!

Thank you so much in advance!

My code looks like this (X and Y are 0/1, the rest is continuous; XW is X*W in the dataframe; MV is M*V in the dataframe):

modmedmod2<- ' # regressions
M ~ a1*X+control1+control2+control3
Y ~ b1*M
Y ~ b2*V
Y ~ b3*MV
M ~ a2*W
M ~ a3*XW
Y ~ cdash*X+control4+control5

# mean of  W (for use in simple slopes)
W ~ W.mean*1
V ~ V.mean*1

# variance of moderators (for use in simple slopes)
W ~~ W.var*W
V ~~ V.var*V

# indirect effects conditional on moderators
indirect.WLVL := a1*b1 + a3*b1*(W.mean-sqrt(W.var))+a1*b3*(V.mean-sqrt(V.var))+a3*b3*(W.mean-sqrt(W.var))*(V.mean-sqrt(V.var))
indirect.WLVM := a1*b1 + a3*b1*(W.mean-sqrt(W.var))+a1*b3*V.mean+a3*(W.mean-sqrt(W.var))*b3*V.mean
indirect.WLVH := a1*b1 + a3*b1*(W.mean-sqrt(W.var))+a1*b3*(V.mean+sqrt(V.var))+a3*(W.mean-sqrt(W.var))*b3*(V.mean+sqrt(V.var))

indirect.WMVL := a1*b1 + a3*W.mean*b1+a1*b3*(V.mean-sqrt(V.var))+a3*W.mean*b3*(V.mean-sqrt(V.var))
indirect.WMVM := a1*b1 + a3*W.mean*b1+a1*b3*V.mean+a3*W.mean*b3*V.mean
indirect.WMVH := a1*b1 + a3*W.mean*b1+a1*b3*(V.mean+sqrt(V.var))+a3*W.mean*b3*(V.mean+sqrt(V.var))

indirect.WHVL := a1*b1 + a3*(W.mean+sqrt(W.var))*b1+a1*b3*(V.mean-sqrt(V.var))+a3*(W.mean+sqrt(W.var))*b3*(V.mean-sqrt(V.var))
indirect.WHVM := a1*b1 + a3*(W.mean+sqrt(W.var))*b1+a1*b3*V.mean+a3*(W.mean+sqrt(W.var))*b3*V.mean
indirect.WHVH := a1*b1 + a3*(W.mean+sqrt(W.var))*b1+a1*b3*(V.mean+sqrt(V.var))+a3*(W.mean+sqrt(W.var))*b3*(V.mean+sqrt(V.var))'

messages.subject_clean: Hayes Model 21 in lavaan: how to implement second stage interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

M and V are both observed, so M*V is calculated from raw data. I am not sure why you think M would be calculated from the first regression.

Consider their Model 4: if the second stage would be calculated based on fitted M, that fitted value would be perfectly collinear with X and estimating the regression would be impossible.

Mikko

messages.subject: Unable to Specify Interaction with Latent variable
messages.subject_clean: Unable to Specify Interaction with Latent variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm new to lavaan and have been working on a growth model. I've been trying to specify an interaction with a latent variable (TrainingChange with AQscore) but have been unable to do so. See my model diagram and code as well as the parameter estimates.
Here is my model:

Here is my code:
#Change model
CM.3 =
  'Train1 =~ 1*TrainingSCRTBlock1
Train6 =~ 1*TrainingSCRTBlock6
TrainChange =~ 1*Train6
TransferPre =~ 1*TransferSCRTPre
TransferPost =~ 1*TransferSCRTPost
TransferChange =~ 1*TransferPost

#Variance/Covariance
Train1~~Train1
TrainChange~~TrainChange
Train1~~TrainChange
Train6 ~~ 0*Train6
TransferPre~~TransferPre
TransferChange~~TransferChange
TransferPre~~TransferChange
TransferPost ~~ 0*TransferPost
TrainingSCRTBlock1 ~~ 0*TrainingSCRTBlock1
TrainingSCRTBlock6 ~~ 0*TrainingSCRTBlock6
TransferSCRTPre ~~ 0*TransferSCRTPre
TransferSCRTPost ~~ 0*TransferSCRTPost
Train1 ~~ TransferPre
SPQscore ~~ SPQscore
SPQscore ~~ AQscore
AQscore ~~ AQscore

#Regression Relations
Train6 ~ 1*Train1
TransferPost ~ 1*TransferPre
TransferChange ~ TrainChange + SPQscore + AQscore + TrainChange*AQscore
Train1 ~ SPQscore + AQscore
TrainChange ~ SPQscore + AQscore

#Intercepts
Train1~1
TrainChange~1
TransferPre~1
TransferChange~1
SPQscore ~ 1
AQscore ~ 1
'

fit.CM.3=lavaan(model=CM.3,data=HW3onyxdat,fixed.x=F)
summary(fit.CM.3)
fitMeasures(fit.CM.3, fit.measures = "all")

Specifically when I identify the interaction in the model figure is DeltaT*AQ. [In the code it is under Regress: TransferChange ~ TrainChange + SPQscore + AQscore + TrainChange*AQscore]

The result below gives me the same estimate as if just specified AQscore, although the parameter is renamed AQscore (TrnC).

Any suggestions; any information that i'm leaving out that would be helpful in diagnosing the problem?

messages.body_plain:
This is straightforward to do, but why do you need it to be negative (or positive). The value of the covariance comes from the data.

Here's how to do it:

y_78 ~~ c1 * y_89 # sets up the covariance and labels it
# constraints
c1 < 0

Note that this also makes your df weird, and so you might not get a chi-square p-value.

Jeremy

messages.subject: SEM with composite variable in more than one regression
messages.subject_clean: SEM with composite variable in more than one regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to fit a composite variables (composed by the variables PCAsp1 and PCAsp2) in a SEM without latent variables. The difficult part is that I want to include the composite variable in three regressions equations. I cannot use the same composite variables in all three equations, so I made three separate composite variables. I already tried to do it with the lavaan syntax for composite variables and according to the method of Grace et al, 2016 in Nature. Both methods give me errors.

#####Method 1: Grace et al 2016
#First, SEM without composites
sem.equations1a <-  '
LAI ~ basal_area + PCAsp1 + PCAsp2
root_biomass ~  basal_area + PCAsp1 + PCAsp2
Biomass_Production ~  PCAsp1 + PCAsp2 + basal_area + HLI + LAI + HLI:LAI+ root_biomass
'

#Then I define 3 composite variables, each composed by the variables PCAsp1 and PCAsp2, based on the coefficients from step 1
resdata[,"SDonLAI"]<- (-0.01704963)*resdata[,"PCAsp1"] -0.07232963*resdata[,"PCAsp2"]
resdata[,"SDonRB"]<- 0.04455446*resdata[,"PCAsp1"] -0.2166291*resdata[,"PCAsp2"]
resdata[,"SDonBP"]<- 0.08209257*resdata[,"PCAsp1"] +0.1704740*resdata[,"PCAsp2"]

#Then I run the model again with composites
sem.equations1b <-  '
LAI ~ basal_area + SDonLAI
root_biomass ~  basal_area + SDonRB
Biomass_Production ~ basal_area + SDonBP + HLI + LAI + HLI:LAI+ root_biomass
'

#But of course, I get the error that my sample cov matrix is not positive definite (multicollinearity problem)
Error in lav_samplestats_icov(COV = cov[[g]], ridge = ridge, x.idx = x.idx[[g]],  :
  lavaan ERROR: sample covariance matrix is not positive-definite

#####Method 2: lavaan syntax (also using the coefficients of step 1 in method 1
sem.equations2 <-  '
Comp1 <~ -0.01704963* PCAsp1 + PCAsp2
Comp2 <~ 0.04455446* PCAsp1 + PCAsp2
Comp3 <~ 0.08209257*PCAsp1 + PCAsp2

LAI ~ basal_area + Comp1
root_biomass ~  basal_area + Comp2
Biomass_Production ~ basal_area + Comp3 + HLI + LAI + HLI:LAI+ root_biomass
´

But then I get this error:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!
  lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

Is there any other way to do this?

Thanks,

Koenraad

I have not tried, but I imagine with some clever constraints in lavaan you could create new parameters representing these quantities and get lavaan to compute the standard errors as well.

messages.subject: Goodness of Fit and Model Adaptation Lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Goodness of Fit and Model Adaptation Lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

 I am currently working on a theory building mixed-methods paper  in which I estimate a structural equation path model based on suggestive paths and links drawn from qualitative in-depth interviews. Based on existing literature and the insights from my qualitative analyses, I have built a structural equation model that is composed of the following:
1) One binary predictor variable (non-latent)
2) 1 latent outcome variable with three items (ordinal scale)
3) 1 latent variable with seven items (ordinal scale)
4) 1 latent variable with two items (continuous scale)
5) 1 latent variable with 14 items (ordinal scale)
6) 1 latent variable with 10 items (ordinal scale)

The sample size is 522 and for each of the latent variables, individual items are highly significant. However, goodness of fit for the full SEM (as well as for some of the individual measurement models for latent variables) is not optimal. According to CFI , model fit is very good (CFI=0.986), but according to RMSEA (=0.103) and SRMR (=0.104) it is rather poor,  also chi2 is 323404.72*** with df=754 indicates poor fit.

I have already inspected modification indices and correlated some error terms, but the model fit could not be  improved substantially. The model is very much embedded in theory and corresponds to my qualitative findings and I am therefore hesitant to discard it altogether. I was wondering whether you have any advice on how to address this issue and could share your thoughts on the following questions:

1) Do you think the above fit statistics are 'too bad' to include the model in a paper/send it to a journal?
2) Is there any reason for why model fit looks good according to CFI but poor according to RMSEA and SRMR? Where does this difference come from?
3) Do you have any other advice on how to possibly refine the model without neglecting theoretical foundations?

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: How do you fix observed variable residuals equal to 1
messages.subject_clean: How do you fix observed variable residuals equal to 1
messages.body_plain:
Diego,
  Your question has not garnered a response.  So, here goes.  You are asking how to do something that it seems unlikely that you want to do.  As such, it seems irresponsible to simply give concise instructions.  Instead, I will consider some alternatives and the conditions under which they might make sense.

  It is a basic assumption of the model that residuals have an expected value, and thus a mean, of zero.  If all the residuals equal 1, this is equivalent to having a mean of 1 and a standard deviation (and thus variance) of 0, which violates the assumption that the mean is zero.  Nonetheless, you can imagine adding 1 to all of your variables and fitting the model with the residuals constrained to 0 and this would be equivalent to having the residuals fixed to 1.  Adding a constant will not change the covariance matrix, so the estimates would all be the same as if you analyzed your original data without adding 1 to each variable.  To set the variances of the residuals to zero, simply avoid specifying them as free parameters.  However, you can do this explicitly as follows.

x ~~ 0 * x

  There are two things to look out for.  First, if any two observed variables share the same causes in such a model, they will have exactly the same values (because you have removed the variances unique to each variable).  This means that you cannot estimate the parameters by any method that requires inverting the covariance matrix.  Second, if you have any latent variable in your model that affects only one observed variable, this latent variable can be interpreted as a residual that violates your constraints.  So, fixing residuals to 1 probably only makes sense if neither of these two conditions apply to your model.  You may violate the first condition if you do not need to estimate the parameters or sill do so by some unusual method that permits a non-positive-definite covariance matrix.

A common mistake is to confuse the residuals with the residual variances.  I do not know whether you made this mistake but this offers a second hypothesis that what you actually wanted to do was fix the residual variances to 1.  You can do this as follows.

x ~~ 1 * x

However, again, you need to be careful about this.  The model underlying lavaan implicitly fixes the loadings of the residuals to 1.  So, fixing the variance to 1 imposes a substantive constraint on the model that seems very unlikely to hold.  The customary model applies to covariances and thus the residual variance could be .1, 1, 10, 100, or any non-negative value.  It would be very unusual for all the residual variances to just happen to equal 1.

Another possibility is that what you have in mind is some form of standardized model.  In that case, fixing the residual variance to 1 would most likely imply that a variable has no causes in the model, in which case it is exogenous and need not even be included in the model (see fixed.x = TRUE in the lavOptions help file).  It is more likely that what you have in mind is that the variance of the observed variable is fixed to 1 which would involve fixing the residual variance to 1 minus the implied variance (which in turn requires taking steps to assure that the implied variance is less than one).

In this case, it may be easier to instead estimate the raw coefficients without the constraints and then request a standardized solution, allowing lavaan to rescale the raw estimates into standardized estimates for you.

summary(yourFitObject, standardized=TRUE)

Another possibility is that you do not mean to fix the residual loadings to 1.  Because the underlying model assumes that these are 1, this requires some respecification.  The steps are as follows:  (1) fix the default residual varances to zero to remove them from the model, (2) specify replacement latent variables to represent residual variances, (3) fix the variance of these replacement variables to 1, and (4) freely estimate the loadings/effect coefficients.  The covariances of these variables will all other exogenous variables should be fixed to zero.  However, you can accomplish the same thing more directly within the model by retaining the default unit loadings and constraining the residual variances to be less than or equal to zero.

For sample code, see my January 26 response to the thread "fixing error variances from 0 to 1."

The default estimator depends upon other characteristics of your model.  You can override this using the 'estimator' parameter when you fit your model.  See the lavOptions help file.

HTH,
Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Alternative way of scaling the underlying variables for categorical indicator items
messages.subject_clean: Alternative way of scaling the underlying variables for categorical indicator items
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

My name is Ai, I have two questions and hope to get some insights.

My first question is short and simple: has the mixture modeling feature been added to the newest version of lavaan? I was hoping to run a set of growth mixture models, and was wondering if that would be possible.

If not, I guess my second question matters for my analysis:

If we are fitting a CFA model using categorical indicator items, we know that in general there are two choices one can make in scaling the underlying variables. One is to set the first threshold of each indicator to zero and freely estimate the intercept of the equation that links the underlying variable (of each indicator) with the latent factor; the other is to set the intercepts to zero and freely estimate the thresholds. What seemed to be the default in lavaan (also in Mplus) is the latter. In addition, the mean of the latent factor is set to zero by default. But I was able to use lavaan to estimate the mean of the latent factor as well as the intercept of categorical indicators if I force the model to follow the other scaling method by using the following constraints: fix the first threshold of each indicator at zero and freely estimate the remaining thresholds, fix the intercept of the scaling item at zero and freely estimate the intercepts of all nonscaling items. However, I cannot apply this approach in Mplus because it wont allow me to estimate the intercepts.

So my question to you is: how did lavaan

manage to estimate this model?  I wanted to ask because I was wondering if I could figure out a way to test the same model in Mplus if I need to switch back for mixture modeling.

Thanks!

Ai

messages.subject_clean: Custom standard errors for covariance matrix input
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm trying to use lavaan to decompose the additive genetic covariances between variables along a particular path diagram (no latent variables). The additive genetic covariances are estimated externally and input into lavaan as a covariance matrix.

The external model also gives estimated standard errors for the AG covariances, and I would like to input these into lavaan (they are much larger than the standard errors for ordinary covariances with the same sample size). I am hoping that lavaan can use these to calculate standard errors for path coefficients and composite variables.

Is there any way to do this? As far as I can tell, lavaan only takes sample sizes as input, not standard errors. Of course, I could write a script to fudge the sample size input so that lavaan standard errors are approximately correct, but this seems like a very inelegant (and not completely general) solution.*

Grateful for any help anyone can offer.

Cheers,
Jono

*A related question - how does lavaan calculated the standard errors of variances of exogenous variables given a covariance matrix as input? The normal approximation of 2sigma^2/(n-1) seems to differ slightly from what lavaan calculates.

Hi all,

I encountered problems accessing standardized summary output when using runMI, as described here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/4FUDQdyniO0

Following the suggested solution, I re-installed semTools and Lavaan using this code:

install.packages("lavaan", repos = "http://www.da.ugent.be", type = "source")
install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

This solved the standardized output issue, but I'm now unable to access fit indices or use the chi argument.

Using the classic Holzinger & Swineford data, with added missingness:

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

HSMiss <- HolzingerSwineford1939[,paste("x", 1:9, sep="")]
randomMiss <- rbinom(prod(dim(HSMiss)), 1, 0.1)

Syntax is correct, but clearly a positive variance is not the maximum likelihood estimate for your data.  As you can see in your output, the estimate is zero, although the machine-precision in this case was a little to the left instead of a little to the right of zero.

Constrained estimation is not a good idea.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150

Better to test whether the negative variance can be explained by sampling error

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138

If your model fits well and the CI includes positive values, then you can dismiss it as sampling error.  Constraining it to be positive will just bias your other estimates and the model-fit test statistic.

This does not specify an interaction.  It tells lavaan to regress TransferChange on AQscore, and to label that slope "TrainChange".  See about Parameter Labels in the tutorial:

messages.subject: Re: Goodness of Fit and Model Adaptation Lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Goodness of Fit and Model Adaptation Lavaan
messages.body_plain:
> 1) Do you think the above fit statistics are 'too bad' to include the model in a paper/send it to a journal?

Depends on your reviewers.

> 2) Is there any reason for why model fit looks good according to CFI but poor according to RMSEA and SRMR? Where does this difference come from?

Different indices tell you different things.  CFI is telling you that the hypothesized model is WAY better than a model that posits zero correlations between any of the variables.  RMSEA is telling you that all of the misfit, spread out across all the model's df, is higher than is typically desired.  SRMR is telling you that the model-implied (Pearson, polychoric, or polyserial) correlations differ by more than 0.1, on average, from the "observed" ones (or estimated ones for categorical data).

> 3) Do you have any other advice on how to possibly refine the model without neglecting theoretical foundations?

Global fit measures are not very informative about why your model fails.  So look for local fit measures.  I like looking at the correlation residuals (SRMR is the average of all of them, which is uninformative), because they tell you which specific bivariate relationships are under/overestimated by the fitted model.

resid(fit, type = "cor")

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> Is there any way to do this? As far as I can tell, lavaan only takes sample sizes as input, not standard errors.

> Quick follow up question - I wonder if anyone has any advice on performing multigroup SEM on imputed data, specifically whether each group to later be compared using multigroup SEM should be imputed separately then recombined before running the multigroup analysis?

Less data means less precision (i.e., more variability) in the imputed values, but imputing groups separately will preserve (on average) any between-group differences in covariance structure, which would be hard to capture otherwise.

> I am very much still learning about R and imputation, and so far I have seen this course recommended (but only on stack exchange etc., and I haven't been able to find any supporting references for this), but been unable to work out how this could be done using mice, semTools, and lavaan.

In Amelia, there is an argument for a grouping variable so that imputation will be performed per group, then combined automatically (I think the argument is "cs=").  Using mice(), I think you would have to impute separate data frames per group, then combine them after.  Use the subset() function to save a data frame per group, impute them, then use a for-loop in which you:
use the complete() function to save each imputed data set back into a data frame (one per imputation)
use rbind() to stack each group's data frame.

> is it posible to introduce this variable in the model using a balanced coding (1, 0, -1) corresponding to the three levels of the variable?

Your strategy will treat it as a continuous variable with linear effect (i.e., one slope, assuming the same amount of change between -1 and 0 as between 0 and 1).  If that is what you want, go for it.  If you think group differences could differ (nonlinear effect), then I would create a dummy code for positive and negative, use both as predictors (neutral would be the reference group).

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm unsure which program you are using to get your measures of additive genetic variance.  My institute has been developing a toolbox for this approach for a little while now that should help. I will echo the DWLS squares approach in general. However, I would caution against using the standard errors to judge the accuracy of your model and (I believe) that you will find using the Chi-square difference test will be more robust when you transition into the simulation stage of your project.  If you like, I can send you the tool kit once its preprint is available?  If you continue using lavaan, try the Chi-square test as an alternative.

Alex

On Wednesday, February 14, 2018 at 4:13:29 AM UTC-7, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Here acov.matrix is the square of the matrix of estimated standard errors from the external model (I think this makes sense?)
>
> Squared SEs (on the diagonal), yes.
>
> > Unfortunately it doesn't seem to matter what the value of acov.matrix is - lavaan's estimates of the standard errors remain the same. Am I making a very basic error? I'm not sure what format the ACOV matrix is meant to be in. I couldn't understand the lavaan documentation on this point.
>
> I haven't used this option before, so maybe Yves can chime in about its use.  Perhaps you need to set the option se="none" so that lavaan() will not calculate SEs in the usual way.
>

> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

#Data grup dengan parameter sama

messages.subject: CFA WLSMV estimator with categorical indicators
messages.subject_clean: CFA WLSMV estimator with categorical indicators
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am conducting a large project to evaluate model fit of a four-factor model. The four-factor model contains 92 categorical items. Each item has two response options, but these options are not ordinal, instead they are binary (0 and 1). I collected over 20K responses from 15 different countries. There are two questions I want to answer. First, does the four-factor model fit the combined sample well? Second, does the four-factor model fit all country/area subgroups well?

I followed the instructions and recommendation of lavaan package and other resources. Basically, I converted the response from 1 and 2 to 0 and 1, and performed a listwise deletion. For the estimator, I used WLSMV, which is claimed to be the most appropriate estimation for categorical data. There's no warning for the combined sample, but I got many pieces of warning when running country/area subgroups. By the way, all subgroups have N > 250 (however, given the number of indicators, 92, and factors, 4, this N is apparently insufficient).

Let's take the Australia sample (N = 776) as an example. I got two warnings:
1. Error in nlminb(start = start.x, objective = minimize.this.function, gradient = GRADIENT,  :
    NA/NaN gradient evaluation
2. In lav_samplestats_from_data(lavdata = lavdata, missing = lavoptions$missing,  :

    lavaan WARNING: number of observations (776) too small to compute Gamma
When I got the first warning, R cannot calculate anything for me. However, if there is only the second warning (for example, U.S. sample N = 3,000), R can calculate what I need (e.g., fit indices). So my first question is that what does the first warning mean and how can I fix it? (P.S. I examined the response pattern, it's good).

The lavaan PDF says "lavaan will automatically switch to the WLSMV estimator: it will use diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) to estimate model parameters, but it will use the full weighted matrix to compute robust standard error, and a mean- and variance-adjusted test statistics." So my second question is that "which function test statistic (chi-square) should I report, DWLS or Robust?" (See the example below).

lavaan (0.5-23.1097) converged normally after 458 iterations

  Number of observations                           634

  Estimator                                       DWLS      Robust
  Minimum Function Test Statistic            10164.685    6863.405
  Degrees of freedom                              4088        4088
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000       0.000
  Scaling correction factor                                  2.526
  Shift parameter                                         2840.064
    for simple second-order correction (Mplus variant)

Thanks you so much!
Yang

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am having a related problem with including auxiliary variables for FIML estimation with "lavaan" and "semTools." I have a longitudinal design with 2 timepoints. The retention rate from T1 (n = 3000) to T2 (n = 2000) is about 66%. I want to conduct a CFA on a measure at T2; however, I want to include T1 measures as auxiliary variables (e.g., one's that predict missingness). I used the "cfa.auxiliary" function below:

auxvars <- c("depression_1","anxiety_1","alcohol_1","drugs_1")
mod <- "extraversion_2 =~ extra1_2 + extra2_2 + extra3_2 + extra4_2"
cfa.auxiliary(mode = mod, aux = auxvars, data = dat, fixed.x = F, meanstructure = T, estimator = "ML", missing = "FIML")

The model runs and converges fine, but I get the following warning about empty cases:
Warning message:
In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some cases are empty and will be ignored:
  2 3 4 5 6 8 9 11 12 13 17 19 22 23 24 25 30 31 32 33 35 38 39 42 45 46 50 52 55 57 61 62 64 66 68 69 70 71 74 75 76 78 79 80 81 82 85 86 89 91 92 94 95 100 101 102 103 104 106 108 109 111 113 115 117 119 120 131 132 134 136 137 140 142 149 152 155 158 162 164 165 166 167 170 172 181 182 184 185 186 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 196 197 198 200 205 207 208 209 213 216 218 220 221 222 224 225 227 228 231 232 235 236 242 245 246 247 249 250 253 257 261 263 264 266 268 275 276 278 279 283 285 287 288 289 290 293 297 298 303 304 306 310 311 312 313 315 316 321 324 325 328 329 330 332 334 335 340 343 344 348 349 350 353 359 360 369 372 375 380 383 385 386 389 390 391 392 394 396 397 398 400 403 406 409 410 411 413 414 415 420 421 422 424 425 426 427 429 431 433 434 435 437 438 442 443 446 448 451 452 453 454 455 456 458 460 465 466 467 468 469 470 471 472 475 477 478 479 480 481 483 486 487 488 492 493 494 495 496 498 501 502 505 506  [... truncated]

I am worried that lavaan is deleting the 1000 cases that only have data at T1 since they are missing for "extra1_2", "extra2_2", "extra3_2", and "extra4_2" (n = 2000). The auxiliary variables all have no missing data (n = 3000) so the full dataframe in the CFA of "extra1_2", "extra2_2", "extra3_2", "extra4_2","depression_1","anxiety_1","alcohol_1","drugs" should have no empty cases. So I am not sure why lavaan would tell me some cases were empty and therefore deleted.

I would love to get people's thoughts,
David

On Thursday, July 13, 2017 at 12:14:54 PM UTC-4, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Obviously I have to always include the auxiliary1 variable which is related to missingness in the outcome , but what about the auxiliary2?
> > For example in the last two models where the effect of predicor3 is constrained to 0 do I have to include the auxiliary2 variable that is related to missingness in predictor3 or not?
>
> Yes, in order to have valid chi-squared difference tests using anova(), you need to fit the model to the same data (observations and variables).
>
> > Also, in models where some predictors are constrained to 0 do I still have to correlate these variables to the auxiliary variables?
>
> Yes.  The correlation with your auxiliary has nothing to do with your hypothesized relationship you test between the predictor and outcome.  You want to make sure the auxiliary correlation is still estimated, so you are only testing the constraint you are interested in.
>
> > I am also guessing that it is ok to work with predictor variables with missing data in lavaan and it is uniform in how it treats missing predictor variables and does not default to excluding cases with missing data on the predictor variables?
>
> Yes, if you set fixed.x = FALSE so that the exogenous predictors are treated as random variables whose (co)variances are freely estimated.  If you are using the auxiliary() function in semTools package, that option will be set automatically,  but you can use it as an argument to a lavaan() function as well.
>

> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics

Hi Mira,

The first warning might be driving everything you're seeing. ML estimation gets "finicky" when variables are on very different scales (e.g. variances differ by a factor of 100 or 1000). My guess the issue is that the products you're using are the culprits. I'd look at the variances in the data and see which variables have (very) large and small variances. Then consider if you can rescale the variables to be on similar scales (I'd do the rescaling first and then recompute the product terms).

Alex

Thank you so much for your invaluable help with this. Following your advice, I now have a suitably imputed dataset, and am able to extract standardized parameter estimates.

I do still seem to be getting an error ("Error in A1 %*% Gamma.g : non-conformable arguments") when I try to extract fit measures for an SEM using my entire dataset, but not when the SEM includes a grouping variable – clearly, I am still doing something wrong!

I have included a reproducible example, and would really appreciate any guidance as to my error(s?!).

I am using:
R version 3.4.2 (2017-09-28)
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)
Running under: Windows 7 x64 (build 7601) Service Pack 1
semTools_0.4-15.913    lavaan_0.6-1.1186   Amelia_1.7.4     Rcpp_0.12.12     bindrcpp_0.2

Example:

#---------------------------------------
# Setting up example data and models
#---------------------------------------

library(semTools)
HSMiss <- HolzingerSwineford1939[ , c(paste("x", 1:9, sep = ""),
                                      "ageyr","agemo","school")]
set.seed(12345)
HSMiss$x5 <- ifelse(HSMiss$x5 <= quantile(HSMiss$x5, .3), NA, HSMiss$x5)
age <- HSMiss$ageyr + HSMiss$agemo/12
HSMiss$x9 <- ifelse(age <= quantile(age, .3), NA, HSMiss$x9)

HS.model <- '

visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6

x8 ~ textual + visual + x9'

#------------------------------------------------------------------
# Imputation
#------------------------------------------------------------------

library(Amelia)
imputed <- amelia(HSMiss, m=30, seed = 12345, cs = "school")
imp.list <- imputed$imputations #make list of dataframes

#------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model estimation - whole sample & by group
#------------------------------------------------------------------

fit <- sem.mi(HS.model, data = imp.list, estimator = "mlm")
fit_group <- sem.mi(HS.model, data = imp.list, estimator = "mlm", group = "school")

anova(fit, test = "D3", indices = TRUE) #"Error in A1 %*% Gamma.g : non-conformable arguments"
anova(fit_group, test = "D3", indices = TRUE)

Furthermore, when I run the same analysis using the non-imputed Holzinger & Swineford data for comparison, I seem to extract quite different fit indices then when using the imputed data. My understanding from reading through the references mentioned in posts on this forum/semTools documentation was that the fit indices on imputed/non-imputed data are comparable (e.g. such as when using the following method) but I now assume I fundamentally misunderstanding something?

#------------------------------------------------------------------
# Analysis on non-imputed data (for comparison)
#-------------------------------------------------------------------

fit_group1 <- sem(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "mlm", group = "school")
fitMeasures(fit_group1) #very different fit indicies

Thanks again for any advice/references/help you can offer.

messages.body_plain:
Standardization is a rescaling method, but one I probably wouldn't recommend (since you're then treating an estimate of a Sd as a known population SD). Rescaling might be as easy as dividing the variable(s) on the largest scale by 10.

Standardizing categorical variables doesn't make a ton of sense to me. I'd only rescale the variables with the largest variances.

Having categorical variables as moderators might be leading to the other errors too. All the work on product indicator approaches I've seen assumes the indicators are continuous. If you have a single categorical variable that you believe is a mediator then it would be easier to use a multiple group approach to testing the interactions instead of a product indicator approach.

messages.body_plain:
Han

I havent seem ECVI tested in simulations, other fits like CFI, TLI, RMSEA, gammahat has been tested more often

Depending on which indices are failling you could consider different reasons, for example, CFI and TLI are affected by the magnitude of correlations between items, if the correlations are very low beteen items CFI and TLI are going to be artifficualy low, if the correlations are very high tey will be artifially high.

You can see papers like
        Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of Fit Indices to Model Misspecification and Model Types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864
         West, S. G., Taylor, A. B., & Wu, W. (2012). Model fit and model selection in structural equation modeling. In R. H. Hoyle (Ed.), Handobook of Structural Equation Modeling (pp. 209–231). New York, NY, US: Guilford Press.
         Browne, M. W., & Cudeck, R. (1992). Alternative Ways of Assessing Model Fit. Sociological Methods & Research, 21(2), 230–258. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124192021002005

Regarding the ECVI for the saturated model you can do something like this: (using the lavaan example fro the cfa function)

library(lavaan)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,std.lv <http://std.lv>=T)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit)
fitMeasures(fit)["ecvi"]

hs_saturated <- '
x1 ~~ x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9
x2 ~~ x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9
x3 ~~ x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9
x4 ~~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9
x5 ~~ x6 + x7 + x8 + x9
x6 ~~ x7 + x8 + x9
x7 ~~ x8 + x9
x8 ~~ x9
'

fit_sat <- cfa(hs_saturated, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit_sat, fit.measures=TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit_sat)
fitMeasures(fit_sat)["ecvi"]

messages.subject_clean: Creating Composits/Formative Latent Variables with Ordinal Observed Variables
messages.body_plain:
lavaan is a package for factor-based SEM. Composites are not factors, so your functionality would be limited, even if your variables were interval or ratio scaled. No, you cannot meaningfully add categorical variables together. You could transform your categorical variables into dichotomous dummy variables and use those collectively to represent the original categorical variables. You could use the "blcok variable" method of Heise (see attached) to capture the joint effects of the transformed categorical predictors, and use that as the effect of the "composite" you want to create.

> anova(fit_group, test = "D3", indices = TRUE)

The problem with the single-group model occurs when anova() has to fit a baseline model for incremental fit indices.  Currently, I pass the name of the grouping variable found with lavInspect(fit, "group"), which is an empty character vector for single-group models.  What I did not foresee is that an empty character vector does not pass lavaan's test: is.null(group), which is used to decide whether to set a default: meanstructure = TRUE (for multigroup models) or FALSE (for single-group models using ML).  I think the error occurs because the baseline model does not estimate any means, despite setting meanstructure = TRUE.

So, this will currently work either (1) if you set meanstructure = TRUE when you first fit your model, or (2) if you don't request any incremental fit indices, for example:

anova(fit, test = "D3", indices = c("srmr","rmsea"))

I'll fix this bug in the coming weeks, when I have time for programming again.  I'll try to remember to post an update here when it is fixed, so you can install the next version.

> Furthermore, when I run the same analysis using the non-imputed Holzinger & Swineford data for comparison, I seem to extract quite different fit indices then when using the imputed data. My understanding from reading through the references mentioned in posts on this forum/semTools documentation was that the fit indices on imputed/non-imputed data are comparable (e.g. such as when using the following method) but I now assume I fundamentally misunderstanding something?
>
>
> #------------------------------------------------------------------
> # Analysis on non-imputed data (for comparison)
> #-------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> fit_group1 <- sem(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "mlm", group = "school")
> fitMeasures(fit_group1) #very different fit indicies

Here, your culprit is the fixed.x argument which is set to TRUE by default in lavaan (so the exogenous X9 is not treated as a random variable, nor is its mean/variance estimated in either group, hence the 4-df difference between models), but runMI() sets it to FALSE by default so that there is no need to assume exogenous variables had complete data (and therefore do not vary across imputations).

> lavInspect(fit_group, "options")$fixed.x
[1] FALSE
> lavInspect(fit_group1, "options")$fixed.x
[1] TRUE

If you set fixed.x = FALSE when you run the sem() function, your npar and df will match the runMI() results.  The indices still look pretty different, but I cannot intuit whether that has anything to do with the way I pool chi-squared for robust test statistics.  I take the average scaling factor across imputations (i.e., Rubin's rules for pooling estimates) and apply that to the pooled naïve chi-squared (using D2 or D3, whichever is requested).  There hasn't been a formal proposal for pooling robust chi-squared in the literature, nor has there been an empirical investigation of how well it performs.

messages.subject: Re: Using journal article info to replicate a SEM model. Account for scale reliability?
messages.subject_clean: Using journal article info to replicate a SEM model. Account for scale reliability?
messages.body_plain:
> Would it be better for me to incorporate the published scale reliabilities in my analysis, maybe by creating single indicators for each latent and adjusting residual variance?

Probably

> If so, how should I specify this in lavaan?

Calculate your observed variance (V_O), then calculate the unreliability portion of that (reliability is a proportion of variance that is reliable).

If V_O = 4 and reliability is estimated as 0.7, that implies the reliable component (common factor) has a variance of 0.7*4 = 2.8, so the unreliable portion is 4 - 2.8 = 1.2.  You can incorporate that into your lavaan model syntax as a fixed value.

model <- '
factor =~ 1*variable
factor ~~ factor # estimated factor variance will be the reliable portion
variable ~~ 1.2*variable # fixed residual variance to unreliable portion
'

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> 1) How can I compare those two models, because in binary situation, lavaan doesn't print any AIC or BIC statistics.

This is irrelevant in your case because both models are saturated (they have zero degrees of freedom, and therefore have arbitrarily perfect fit).

> Is it correct to compare chisq-values, and say the smaller chisq value the better model (model 6_1: 823.823 vs model7_1:545.740). In this example, model7_1 would be better, right?

You are looking at the values for the baseline model (used to calculate CFI and TLI), not your hypothesized model.

> 2a) How can I interpret estimates?

It is probit regression:

https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/42956/how-do-i-interpret-a-probit-model-in-stata

> 2b) Total effect is 0.232. Probability to get value 1 of variable lapsi_mtke0615_2 under model6_1 is (1dnorm(0.232,0,1)) 0.61156509?

This depends on whether you use delta parameterization (total variance of latent response = 1) or theta parameterization (residual variance of latent response = 1).  But I think you have the right idea.

> 3) What are those thresholds-values. How to interpret them?

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

> 4) Can I multiply estimates in binary case also for example under model6_1, direct effect is (a*b) + (d*e)?

There are some issues that I am not familiar with, but there are some notes you might find useful in this presentation (starting with slide 22):

http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> - lavaan's estimates of the standard errors remain the same. Am I making

The (N)ACOV argument can not be used for this. The purpose of this
argument is to provide a custom 'Gamma' matrix to be used for the
computation of the satorra-bentler test statistic. The direct need for
this was the lavaan.survey package.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Your model is a saturated and recursive model of observed variables. In this case it could be a lot simpler if you just estimated the model with separate logistic regressions. But the interpretation of the model and the choice of modeling strategy depends on what is your interest. Are the variables that you are interested in dichotomous (e.g. biological gender), or are they continuous but measured with dichotomous variables (e.g. a yes/no answer to a question of do you feel sick today.)? These two cases require different approaches and also the interpretation of the mediation effect would be different.

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
Alex,
  Perhaps it is the first part of the error that is confusing you.  This is not that important in this case and is simply telling you that the function lav_samplestats_icov().  The second part is the important part for your purposes.  It is fairly transparent in telling you that your sample covariance matrix cannot be inverted because it is not positive definite.  This is a data problem, not a syntax problem.

  Your later code should help identify the problem.  You tested that the determinant of the covariance matrix was non-negative.  My only suggestion would be to test for greater-or-equal to zero to better match the property of being positive definite.

  It is not necessary but only sufficient for being non-positive definte that one variable perfectly predicts another.  Another possibility is that two or more variables perfectly predict a third.  A convenient way to check for this is to use the rela package to run a classical item analysis on your variables.  Ignore all the output except the squared multiple correlation predicting each variable from the rest.  If any of these is 1, that variable is your problem.  Another possibility is that one of your columns of data is a constant instead of a variable, or becomes one when you address missing data.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject_clean: Interpreting coefficients with categorical endogenous variables
messages.body_plain:
> 1) Could I use nominal variables as endogenous by declaring them as 'factor' variables instead of 'ordered' in R?

lavaan does not support nominal multicategory outcomes

> I'm wondering how I should interpret these coefficients. The estimation method used 'DWLS'. I have also got some threshold parameter. Is there any example that I can see that will help me understand the interpretation?

It is probit regression for the ordinal outcome, linear regression for the continuous outcome.  If you are using the default "delta" parameterization and have a single-group model (or no constraints across multiple groups), then you can interpret the probit slope as a regular linear effect on the assumed standard-normal (i.e., z-score) latent response underlying the observed ordinal response.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Of course. Instead of using slope loadings reflecting equal time intervals, use slope loadings that reflect different time intervals. If test 1 happens at time 0 and test 2 happens at time 4, then set loadings of 0*t1 and 4*t2. You will need to choose and set these values yourself. Bear in mind that your choice of starting point (your choice of a time 0 period) will make a difference in some of your results.

There may be small differences between packages, including the use of n or n - 1 to compute covariances or standard errors, and also differences in "tuning," which may lead different programs to converge on slightly different values for the same data and model. AFAIK, lavaan does not currently include a "mimic" option to better match Amos results.

A Review of Eight Software Packages for Structural Equation Modeling

Hi,

The basic approach is this:

library(lavaan)
library(semTools)

model <- '
  # measurement model
ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
ind60dem60 =~ x1.y1 + x2.y2 + x3.y3

# regressions
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60 + ind60dem60'

fit <- sem(model, data = orthogonalize(PoliticalDemocracy, c("x1", "x2", "x3"), c("y1", "y2", "y3")))
summary(fit, standardized=TRUE)

Different variants of the technique are produced by:
1) adding constraints to loadings, possibly from previously estimated models
2) creating the interaction indicators differently

You can also check out this package, which implements the LMS approach

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nlsem/nlsem.pdf

Alex, Sarah,

Right. I did not read the question thoroughly. I do not think that approximating the latent variables with sums of the indicators is a good idea because it will lead to biased estimates of the original model parameters.

Using the selectively to form the interaction terms should work in principle, but it would be an inefficient approach. One way around this problem would be leveraging the fact that a higher order model is a special case of a bifactor model. (e.g. doi:10.3390/jintelligence5030027), in which case this would reduce to a first level model with appropriate constraints.

But perhaps LMS would be the easiest approach for this.

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: Interpreting coefficients with categorical endogenous variables
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting coefficients with categorical endogenous variables
messages.body_plain:
> Also, could you please suggest me how will be the interpretation for SA2 over SA1, both of which are ordinal?

In a probit model, slopes have the same interpretation whether the outcome has 2, 3, 4... ordered categories.  See below.

> > Do you remember any work that interpreted similar SEM outputs?

Not path analyses, just common-factor and IRT models (where the predictors are latent traits).  But you can search the web for readings about probit regression.  Path analyses are simultaneous regression models, so what you find should generally apply to path models too.

> > If emp1 and emp2 both are binary, should I be able to say "if emp1 changes from 0 to 1, the probability for the variable emp2 taking value one rises by 187.5% points, or other words, almost doubles"?

No, the slopes are not effects on the probability, but linear effects on the latent variable that underlies the discrete observed response.  The slope of 1.875 indicates the latent variable (assumed normally distributed, probably a z score if you use delta parameterization) is 1.875 higher for the emp1==1 group than the emp1==0 group, holding the other covariates constant.  The corresponding change in the probability that emp2==1 will depend on the values at which you hold the other covariates constant (because the intercept is fixed at zero, it won't depend on that).

$$ probit(emp2=1) = 0 + 1.875(emp1) + 0.679(SA1) - 0.057(PHQ8_1) $$

For example, if the covariates both == 0, then the expected probit(emp2==1) is
for emp1==0: 0 + 1.875(0) + 0.679(0) - 0.057(0) = 0
for emp1==1: 0 + 1.875(1) + 0.679(0) - 0.057(0) = 1.875
The cumulative probabilities that correspond to these z-scores are

> pnorm(c(0, 1.875))
[1] 0.5000000 0.9696036

If you hold the covariates constant at different values, you will get different expected values for the probit, and therefore different (differences between) probabilities.

Because SA1 is endogenous, I assume its estimated effect on emp2 is the effect of SA1's underlying latent response, but I am not certain about that.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: monteCarloMed bug with subtraction
messages.subject_clean: monteCarloMed bug with subtraction
messages.body_plain:
> It looks like a bug in the code. I'll get it fixed ASAP.

The problem is the uniquepar() function defined within the monteCarloMed() function.  It only looks for "+" and "*" operators, so it thinks "b1-a1" is the variable name rather than "b1".

> uniquepar('a1*b1-a1*b2')
[1] "a1"    "b1-a1" "b2"

Given that some indirect effects involve more complex functions (e.g., when outcomes are binary, but we'd like to see a CI for indirect effects in an odds-ratio metric: see slide 25 here <http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf>), it would be nice if the function were more general, allowing any R expression that can be calculated on the sampled parameters.

I propose we get rid of the uniquepar() function and replace line 153

paramnames <- uniquepar(expression)

with this:

paramnames <- all.vars(as.formula(paste("~", expression)))

It would work with Mauricio's example:

med <- 'a1*b1 - a1*b2'

all.vars(as.formula(paste("~", med)))
[1] "a1" "b1" "b2"

and in more general cases (e.g., with log(), pnorm(), or ^):

all.vars(as.formula(paste("~", med)))
[1] "a1" "b1" "b2"

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
